pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Thallium Poisoning (Thallium Toxicity) THE SMOKING GUN: The classic triad of severe painful ascending peripheral neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction (tachycardia/hypertension), followed precisely 2 weeks later by sudden diffuse alopecia and Mees' lines on the nails. Standard heavy metal screens test for Lead, Arsenic, and Mercury, but miss Thallium unless specifically ordered. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Thallium monovalent cations share a nearly identical ionic radius with potassium ions. Thallium replaces potassium in the body, actively entering cells via the Na+/K+-ATPase pump. Once intracellular, it exerts toxicity through multiple mechanisms: it binds to sulfhydryl groups on enzymes, inhibits succinate dehydrogenase (disrupting the Krebs cycle and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation), and disrupts protein cross-linking. The high rate of energy consumption in peripheral nerve axons leads to painful axonal degeneration, while the disruption of sulfhydryl-rich keratin synthesis causes sudden hair follicle arrest (anagen effluvium) and transverse nail dystrophy (Mees' lines).
